analysis.one_liner: Gives database companies a new legal right to stop others from reusing the facts they collect.
analysis.headline: The database bill cleared two House committees but was reported by one of them with a recommendation against passage, never received a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a brand-new kind of legal claim, separate from copyright, for companies that assemble large databases of facts — stock prices, sports scores, legal case data, real estate listings. Anyone who republished a substantial chunk of someone else's database without permission could be sued, and courts could shut them down and award damages on top of actual losses. The bill carved out exceptions for news reporting, hyperlinking, government data, and nonprofit schools and research labs, but ordinary reuse of collected facts would have become a lawsuit risk for the first time since the Supreme Court ruled in 1991 that raw facts cannot be copyrighted.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that sell access to large collections of facts — legal, scientific, financial, and real-estate data publishers above all. The bill gave them a federal legal claim against competitors who republish substantial parts of their databases, letting them charge for information that previously could be freely re-reported once obtained, and giving them injunctions, damages of up to three times actual losses, and the power to have copied material impounded and destroyed.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new civil claim against anyone who makes available in commerce a quantitatively substantial part of another person's database without authorization, where the database cost substantial money or time to build, the reuse is time-sensitive, and free riding would threaten the incentive to produce the database.
Gives database owners court injunctions, impoundment and destruction of copied material, actual damages plus attributable profits, and additional damages up to 2 times actual damages.

Fills a gap left after the Supreme Court's Feist decision (1991) held that facts, however much work went into collecting them, are not protected by copyright — a protection proponents argued was needed to keep companies investing in expensive databases.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who reuses or republishes collected facts: small information businesses building competing products, internet services, researchers, journalists, and ultimately the public, which would face new litigation risk and potential paywalls around information previously free to reuse. The bill preempts some state laws on the same conduct, so there would be no alternative route around the new federal claim.

drawbacks.text: The strongest case for the bill was real: after Feist, a company could spend heavily assembling a database and a rival could copy it wholesale, which proponents argued would erode the incentive to build such databases at all. The bill's own liability test — substantial investment, time-sensitive reuse, and threatened incentive — was written to capture exactly that scenario.

The honest cost: the bill attached property-style rights to facts themselves, not expression. Liability would turn on court judgments about what counts as 'substantial,' 'time sensitive,' and 'competition,' inviting litigation against small competitors, information aggregators, and users well beyond the clear-cut free-rider cases, with chilling effects on reuse of factual information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying problem the bill targeted — free-riding on expensive databases — was genuine but narrow. The remedy reached far past it: facts themselves would become privately enforceable property, with courts sorting out the exceptions case by case. Existing contract law, trade secrets, and the narrow 'hot news' doctrine already covered much of the harm proponents cited. Weighed against the cost to open reuse of information — the raw material of research, journalism, and most internet services — the bill traded broad public access for a narrow and redundant layer of industry protection.

outcome.mechanism: Both committees cleared it — Energy and Commerce reported it with a recommendation against passage — and it sat on the House calendar for the rest of the Congress without ever getting a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Howard Coble introduced the bill on October 8, 2003, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The Courts, Internet, and Intellectual Property Subcommittee forwarded it to the full committee on October 16, 2003 by a vote of 10 to 3.
The full Judiciary Committee ordered it reported on January 21, 2004 by a vote of 16 to 7, and it was reported as amended on February 11, 2004.

The bill was then referred sequentially to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which ordered it reported by voice vote on March 3, 2004 and reported it adversely — with a recommendation against passage — on March 11, 2004, alongside its own amendment.
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 252) on March 11, 2004 and was never taken up on the House floor; no further action appears before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet companies, libraries, researchers, and small information businesses that re-use collected facts are better off, because the new legal claim over facts never became law. Database publishers lose the chance to charge for facts that were previously open to republication, and the public keeps the status quo where raw facts are free to reuse.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet firms, libraries, and information reusers

for.name: Rep. Howard Coble
for.role: House sponsor; chairman of the Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through his subcommittee, which forwarded it to the full committee by a 10-3 vote.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the amended bill reported by a 16-7 vote on January 21, 2004 and reported it to the House on February 11, 2004.

for.name: 9 House cosponsors (7 Republicans, 2 Democrats), later joined by 4 additional sponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors and additional sponsors, including Reps. Sensenbrenner, Tauzin, Smith of Texas, Wexler, and Delahunt
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; several held leadership posts on the two committees of jurisdiction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Reported the bill adversely on March 11, 2004 — recommending against passage — while returning it with its own amendment.

against.name: House Republican leadership under Speaker Dennis Hastert
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar; it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Library, research, and scientific communities
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed creating property rights in facts, arguing it would restrict research and public access to information.

against.name: Internet and technology companies
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill, warning that liability for republishing facts would burden the internet economy.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but lopsided — 7 Republicans and 2 Democrats among the original cosponsors, with additional sponsors from both parties added in committee — and committee votes (16-7, 10-3, and a voice vote) mixed members of both parties on both sides.

industries.industry: Database publishers (legal, scientific, financial, and real-estate data)
industries.note: The bill would have handed them a new federal claim against anyone republishing substantial parts of their databases, letting them fence off and charge for facts that were previously free to reuse once obtained. That cost would have landed on researchers, journalists, small competitors, and the public.

The bill exempted interactive computer services from liability for third-party content, but they would still have faced litigation over their own products and services built on factual data. Their interest in open reuse of information ran alongside the public's.

The bill carved out nonprofit educational and scientific uses, but the carve-outs depended on court determinations of reasonableness and were lost where a nonprofit competed commercially. Their core interest was in keeping facts freely reusable, which the bill constrained.

News reporting was exempted, but the exemption lapsed for time-sensitive information used in a consistent pattern of direct competition — a rule aimed squarely at sports scores and fast-moving data resellers, while protecting established news-gathering operations.
